description: We will create something simple that everyone can understand, in order to learn and pass on this knowledge.
summary: NASA has left at least 17 machines on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space, but most students only hear about the missions flying today. Echoes of Space is a free web story collection for students aged 9 to 14 and their teachers. Each machine tells its own story in the first person, from the Apollo 11 descent stage to the Ingenuity helicopter and the Kepler telescope. Every story answers the same six questions: what happened in its own words, why it was sent, how it worked, what it found, why it is still out there, and what it still tells us. The stories use NASA photos and records, with a map pin at each landing site and a link to the NASA source for every fact. It works in English, Spanish, Portuguese and French and can read each story aloud.
details:
Echoes of Space turns NASA's dense technical archives about abandoned hardware into stories students can follow. It covers 17 machines. On the Moon: the Apollo 11 descent stage, Surveyor 3 and the three Apollo rovers. On Mars: Viking 1 and 2, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, InSight and Ingenuity. In deep space: Pioneer 10, NEAR Shoemaker on asteroid Eros, Dawn orbiting Ceres, and Kepler.

Each machine narrates its own story and answers six questions: its story in its own words, why it was sent, how it worked, what it found, why it is still out there, and what it still tells us. Instead of listing facts, every "How it worked" chapter ties one piece of hardware to one result. Eagle's throttled engine let it hover past boulders. Spirit's broken wheel dug up evidence of past water. Dawn's ion engines let it orbit two worlds. Kepler measured dips in starlight to find planets.

The site has four sections. Explorers presents the problem, the six questions and the 17 machines. The Map shows Moon and Mars maps built from NASA global mosaics, with markers at the published landing coordinates. The Timeline compares each machine's real working life with its planned mission. Sources lists every NASA source and photo. A downloadable "Remembered by…" postcard creates a personal connection.

Every fact is linked to NSSDCA or NASA mission pages, and all 57 photos are NASA's, listed with their IDs. The site works on phones and classroom computers, in four languages, with read-aloud, keyboard and reduced-motion support, and with no login or tracking.

It is built as a static HTML, CSS and JavaScript site with Leaflet 1.9.4 in an equirectangular projection, so NASA mosaics map directly to latitude and longitude. It needs no backend. Next steps are adding the ALSEP packages, more Surveyors and Pioneer 11, student-narrated audio, a teacher's guide and more languages.

As a student scrolls through the chapters, the panel beside them changes: a NASA photo, the landing site on a 3D globe built from NASA mosaics, NASA's official 3D model of the spacecraft, and key numbers. A "How far" view shows how far away each machine is today, using NASA/JPL Horizons, how long a radio signal would take to reach it, and how many years it has been silent.
